sources.title: Metabolic basis to Sherpa altitude adaptation
sources.publisher: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
notes: Sherpa-lowlander comparison during exposure to Everest Base Camp conditions found differences in muscle fuel use, oxygen-use efficiency, energetic reserves and oxidative-stress markers.
The study supports a contribution from tissue metabolism but its participant sample was limited, so results should not be treated as universal individual predictions.

sources.title: Genetic Variants in EPAS1 Contribute to Adaptation to High-Altitude Hypoxia in Sherpas
notes: Reports EPAS1-associated genetic variation in Sherpas in relation to adaptation to high-altitude hypoxia.
The associations are population-level evidence and do not alone predict any person's endurance or safety.

sources.title: Down-Regulation of EPAS1 Transcription and Genetic Adaptation of Tibetans to High-Altitude Hypoxia
notes: Functional analysis links Tibetan-enriched EPAS1 variants with down-regulated expression and a comparatively restrained haemoglobin-related response in hypoxia.
The article discusses Tibetan highlanders; applying every finding identically to all Sherpa individuals requires caution.

sources.title: High-Altitude Travel and Altitude Illness
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
notes: CDC travel guidance describes physiological stress and illness risk at altitude and the importance of gradual acclimatization.
Inherited adaptation cannot replace individual ascent planning or attention to symptoms.

sources.title: Sherpa and Tibetan population genetic variation
sources.publisher: National Center for Biotechnology Information, PubMed Central
notes: Population-genetic work examines similarities and differences among Sherpa and Tibetan groups.
Group-level genetic variation is not a deterministic measure of an individual's climbing ability.
